p: It's January 2061. Ares Station, a colony of 212 people in Jezero crater on Mars, is slowly losing its oxygen plant.

Earth's one rescue is the Halcyon, a relief ship being built by Tallgrass Aerospace in Watkins, on the plains east of Denver. It'll carry a new oxygen plant the crew calls the Breather, and four people to install it.

The planets give it one launch window, just over two years away. It opens at the end of January 2063 and closes in early March, and the target date inside it is February 18, 2063. Miss it, and the next window comes twenty six months later, which is too late.

You're Sam Okafor, fifty, a former Air Force F-16 crew chief who has kept Tallgrass's high bay running for nineteen years and has never run a project. His daughter Ada is a hydroponics engineer on the station. They can't talk live, only trade recorded logs.
Every scene ends with a decision. Make the call you'd make. The story remembers.
The people you'll hear from first.
Bea Kowal. The program manager until last Friday, when she walked out of a schedule review.
Quinn Abernathy. The program's scheduler, twenty six.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, the agency paying for the ship.
Garrett Lyle. Founder and CEO of Tallgrass Aerospace, which builds the ship.
New in this chapter: Wendell Price, Hana Iwasaki, Rafa Quintero, Ruth Calder and Ray Mendez.

Monday, January 10, 2061. 5:40 AM. The tablet on the kitchen table made the two note chime it only made for Mars, and Sam Okafor, in his socks at the counter, said Okay, to it out loud, which was a thing he'd started doing and didn't love. The coffee maker had been slow since Thanksgiving. He kept meaning to replace it. He kept not doing it, because Grace had bought it, and he'd never read the manual, and as long as it worked he wouldn't have to.

He had an order for this by now. Coffee. The chair by the back window, where the yard was still dark and the neighbor's motion light clicked on for a rabbit, then for the same rabbit again. Then the tablet. The log had left Jezero crater ten minutes and seven seconds before it got to Aurora. Before that it had sat in the relay queue most of the night, so Ada had said every word of it hours ago, at the end of her shift, on a planet where it was already dark again. Nothing she said was news by the time he heard it. He'd stopped minding that. Mostly.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3518. One way, 10 minutes 7 seconds. Margin, 952 days. Hi, Dad. End of shift. Mom's watch says just after midnight your time, so you'll get this with your coffee, and the coffee maker will be doing that thing where it sighs at you. Get the coffee. I'll wait. I mean, I won't, I'm recorded, but you know what I mean. Good news first. Basil. I've got eleven plants going in cut down sample tubes on the shelf over my bunk, and Dr. Lindgren in medical says it's a fire code violation. I asked her which fire department she was going to call. She took one home. Okay. Real stuff. Stack four lost another two percent this week. That's the third week in a row. Hollis's report to Earth says the plant is operating "within projected degradation," which is true if you projected it on a napkin. I took the actual cell voltages off the plant log and ran the curve myself, three times, on three different fits, because I know what you're going to ask. I get 952 days of margin. His report says 1,012. Sixty days is a lot of days, Dad. It's two months of everybody breathing. Don't tell Hollis I said that. Actually, tell him. No. Don't. I'll tell him. I'll tell him tomorrow. Your last log. You did the voice. The "everything's fine, kiddo, the people over here are top notch" voice. You used that voice for all of junior high. I know what it means. Don't do the voice, Dad. I'm an engineer on a planet that's trying to kill me. I can take a number. And I know Bea's job is a mess, because the feed says "Halcyon program reaffirms schedule" every four days, and nobody reaffirms anything that's fine. Love you. My number's 952. Ada out.

He watched it twice. The second time he paused it where she held up four fingers for stack four, because her nails were bitten down the way they'd been in eighth grade, the year her mother got sick, and he hadn't seen them like that since.

Then he got the gas bill out of the drawer by the phone charger, the drawer that still had Grace's reading glasses in it, folded, on top of the takeout menus, and turned the bill over and wrote 952 on the back. Under it he wrote 969. Everyone at Tallgrass knew that one without thinking: the number of days from this morning to September 6, 2063, when the Halcyon was supposed to reach Mars, if it left on February 18 of the year after next, if it left at all. He subtracted. Then he did it again, the way you check a torque value you don't like.

The ARA's number, the one in Hollis Bayne's reports and on the agency's website and in every briefing Sam had sat in the back of, left the colony forty three days to spare. Ada's number ran the air out seventeen days before the ship got there. He sat with the bill in his hand until the coffee went cold. Then he put it under the fruit bowl, face down, and went to work.

Tallgrass Aerospace was thirty five minutes east on I-70, past the last warehouses and out onto the plains, where the ground goes flat and brown and the wind stops being weather and starts being a fact. You could see the high bay from the interstate, a white box ten stories tall with TALLGRASS down the side in letters a pronghorn could read from Kansas. Inside it, under the cranes, two of the Halcyon's three modules stood in their stands with their skins off. The third, the departure stage, was bolted to the test stand two miles out on the prairie. Sam had kept that building running for nineteen years. He knew which doors stuck in a north wind and which crane drifted left under load. He'd never once been in charge of what got built inside it.

The 7:30 integration standup started without Bea Kowal, the program manager, which had never happened. Her fleece was still on the back of her chair from Friday. Quinn Abernathy, the scheduler, kept looking at it while people talked, as if it might explain itself.

Everyone knew about Friday by then. At the program schedule review, on slide nineteen, Bea had stopped in the middle of a sentence about the Breather's acceptance test and looked at the screen for what Quinn said was a long time. I can't make this true, she'd said, to nobody in particular. Then she closed her laptop, picked up her keys, and walked out past Garrett Lyle and the ARA's deputy director and forty people on the call. Nobody had heard from her since.

At 10:12 Quinn's phone rang and she took it in the hall. When she came back she sat down next to Sam instead of in her own seat. That was her sister. A sheriff's deputy found Bea's car in the grocery store lot in Bennett. Engine running, heater on. She's okay. She isn't hurt. She's just sitting there, and she won't talk to anybody from here. Quinn had both hands flat on the table. Her sister's driving out. She said please don't call her.

Imogen Hale drove out from Denver herself that afternoon, which people noticed, because the Director of the Ares Relief Authority usually made people come to her. She'd been a senator for twelve years before the ARA, and she still walked into a room like there might be a camera in it. In Garrett's corner office, with the window full of brown prairie and the wind sock on the flight control building standing straight out, she didn't sit.
You run the building, she said to Sam. Garrett tells me nothing in it has fallen over in eighteen years.

Nineteen, Garrett said. Every year he's had it. He was smiling. Garrett had started Tallgrass in a rented hangar at twenty nine, and he smiled hardest when he was losing an argument, so Sam had learned to read that smile the way you'd read a gauge.

I need someone running Halcyon by Wednesday, and it has to be someone the people out there will follow. Bea's out. I'm not going to pretend she's back this month, and I'm not putting a consultant from Virginia in front of your engineers. She looked at him. You've never run a project.
You were an F-16 crew chief.
And your daughter is on Ares Station.
He didn't say anything to that.

I'll be straight with you, because I think you'd see through anything else. A project lead with a daughter on Mars is a story the public will understand. I go back to eleven partner governments every year and ask them for more money until that ship leaves. You're part of how I do that.

Garrett's smile went flat for half a second and came back. Sam looked out at the wind sock. He thought about the gas bill under the fruit bowl. He thought about saying no, and he could see exactly how it would go: somebody else in this office by Wednesday, somebody else's hands on the plan, and him at the kitchen table at 5:40 every morning, listening to the margin go down in his daughter's voice, with nothing to do about it but listen.

He understood what she'd told him. Ada was part of the reason. He took it anyway, because it was the only way he was ever going to get his hands on the thing that was supposed to bring his daughter her air.

Driving home he passed the high bay with every light on, the modules inside lit up like something in a church, and a pronghorn standing on the shoulder of the access road, watching the cars go by like it was counting them.
Ruth's Console Log, page one: who can call a hold.

Ruth's console log, 424 days before launch. oh six hundred, badged in. FD console, flow 3. chair wobbles. filed a ticket. oh seven ten, first loop check as Petrel FD. all stations answered. prop answered first. Wendell. of course. oh nine hundred, Arnaud, Mori, Tate in for badge photos. Mori asked if the FD gets a Cape. no. Tate asked who can call a hold. oh nine oh five, list on the whiteboard. FD. test conductor. range. any crew member. any station on this loop. the janitor if he sees smoke. oh nine oh six, short version: everybody. write that down, Ruthie. fourteen hundred, charter signed by the administrator. my name on page 2. authority to hold, scrub, recycle. no authority to move the window. nobody has that one. seventeen thirty, L minus 424. went home. didn't sleep. the good kind.

That's me at forty seven, on the first day of the best job I ever had. I'd wanted that chair since I was nine. I wrote the most important thing on that page at 9:06 in the morning, and then I spent fourteen months forgetting it. You'll get the rest of the pages the same way Sam does, one at a time. I don't hand them out faster because I can't read them any faster.

I'm going to teach you what's on each page, because that's the only use I've found for them. Start with the word at the top of this one. Flow. A flow is what we called a project before somebody gave us the vocabulary. PMI's vocabulary now, and the one your exam uses, is that a project is a temporary initiative in a unique context undertaken to create value. Temporary means it starts and it ends. The Petrel flow started on a Friday in 2034 and it ended, one way or another, on launch day. Unique context means this exact thing, with these people and this planet in this position, hasn't been done before, so you can't run it off last year's checklist. And create value is the part people skip. A project exists because something on the other side of it is worth the effort.

The exam content outline, the ECO, goes further than older editions did on that last part. PMI's research reframed project success. The old scorecard, schedule and budget and scope, still matters. But the outline says a project succeeded when people saw that it delivered value worth the effort and expense. Write that next to my 0906 line. Sam's project has a date on every wall at Tallgrass. The value is 212 people breathing. If those two ever disagree, the value wins, and it's your job to say so out loud.

Operations are the other kind of work: ongoing, repeating, keeping something running. Sam ran operations for nineteen years. The high bay's lights, the cranes, the badge readers. Halcyon is a project that lives inside that building. He knows the difference in his hands. Now he has to know it on paper.
How the exam asks it. If a scenario describes ongoing repeated work, it's operations. If it asks how to judge success, look for value delivered to stakeholders, not only on time and on budget.
The charter, and the things that aren't one.

At 1400 the Administrator signed the Petrel's charter, and my name went on page two. That's the document I want you to understand cold. A project charter formally authorizes the project and names the project manager, and it's where the project manager's authority comes from. The sponsor issues it. The PM often drafts it, which is fine and usually faster, but the sponsor's signature is what makes it real. It's short and high level: why the project exists, what it has to achieve, how you'll know it worked, the big milestones and the money, the major risks and assumptions, the key stakeholders, and what the PM is allowed to decide.

Now the things that get mistaken for a charter, because Sam will meet every one of them this month. A mandate is the political or business decision that something must happen. The ARA's mandate for Halcyon is a press release with Imogen Hale's quote in it, and it's a perfectly good mandate. It doesn't say who's in charge or what they can decide. A contract is a legal agreement between two organizations. Tallgrass's contract with the ARA says what Tallgrass owes the agency. It doesn't tell anybody inside the program that Sam can move an engineer. A statement of work describes the work a supplier will do. A business case is the argument that the investment is worth making. Each of them feeds the charter. None of them replaces it.

Who should sign? The sponsor is the person or group who provides the resources and is accountable for enabling the project's success. On Halcyon that's the ARA, and inside the ARA it's Hale. Garrett runs the prime contractor. He's a crucial stakeholder with a lot of power, and he is not the sponsor of the agency's rescue mission. A charter signed by the contractor's CEO authorizes the contractor. It doesn't authorize the mission.

In agile settings the same purpose is often served by something lighter, a product vision or a one page agreement, and that's tailoring, which PMI encourages. What you can't tailor away is the authorization. Somebody with the authority has to say, in writing, this is ours, and you lead it.

How the exam asks it. "The PM can't get resources released" points back to a missing charter. "Start now and write the charter later" is usually a trap, and so is treating the contract as the charter.
Governance: who decides, and who can stop it.

My 0905 list was governance, though I didn't call it that. Governance is the framework for how decisions get made on a project: who decides what, by what rules, how issues go up when they can't be settled where they are, and how the people above you get told. The ECO's version under B1 says you describe and establish the structure, rules, procedures, reporting, ethics, and policies, using the organization's process assets. It says you define success metrics. And it says you outline escalation paths and thresholds. Underline that last one. A threshold is the line past which a decision isn't yours anymore.

The PMBOK Guide's eighth edition makes governance one of its seven performance domains. Most of the disasters I've seen started as a decision made by the wrong person, or by nobody, because nobody had written down who owned it.

Notice what was on my list and what wasn't. Anyone could call a hold. Only a few people could approve going forward with a known problem. That asymmetry is the whole point. Make stopping cheap and continuing deliberate. The fastest way to get a project into trouble is to reverse that, so that stopping takes three signatures and continuing takes none.

On Halcyon the governance has an extra piece. The ARA's Independent Readiness Board sits outside the program on purpose. It doesn't run the project. It decides whether the ship is ready to fly, and the program can't overrule it. If you're Sam, you want to know on your first day which of your decisions go to that board. If you don't decide that early, somebody will decide it for you, late, in a hurry.
How the exam asks it. When a question asks who should decide something big, the answer is rarely the PM alone. The PM analyzes and recommends. Governance decides, at the level the thresholds set.
Stakeholders, including the ones who can't come to the meeting.

Stakeholders are the people and groups who affect the project or are affected by it. The ECO asks you to identify them, analyze them, categorize them, and tailor how you communicate with each. You do all of that in a stakeholder register: who they are, what they care about, how much influence they have, how engaged they are now, and how engaged you need them to be. That last pair matters more than people think. A key stakeholder who's unaware or resistant today and needs to be supportive by spring is a plan, not a note.

A power and interest grid is the quick way to sort them. High power and high interest, you manage closely. High power and low interest, keep them satisfied without burying them. Low power and high interest, keep them informed. Low power and low interest, keep an eye on them, because that changes.

Here's what my 2034 register got wrong. It listed the agency, the contractors, the crew, and Congress. It didn't list the families. It didn't list the press, who turned out to have more influence over our last month than the Administrator did. Sam's register has 212 people on it who live on another planet and can't come to any meeting he'll ever hold. They're the reason the project exists, and they're also the only stakeholders who'll know before anybody on Earth whether the plan is working, because they're breathing it.
Mars itself goes in the charter, as a constraint. Put the window there, put the colony in the register, and don't confuse the two.

And keep identifying. Stakeholders show up the whole way through. The exam's favorite version is the new department you discover in month four. The answer is never "planning is done." Add them, analyze them, and engage them.
How the exam asks it. A newly discovered stakeholder means you update the register and assess their needs. Ignoring them because the plan is baselined is the trap.

The first People task on the ECO is to develop a common vision. The enablers are plain: help ensure a shared vision with key stakeholders, promote it, keep it current, and when people misunderstand it, find the root cause of the misunderstanding.

A date isn't a vision. I learned that the hard way. Our wall in 2034 had a countdown clock on it, and by the end everybody in that room could tell you the number of days and nobody could tell you what the days were for. A vision says who this is for and what changes for them, in words the team would use themselves. You build it with the people who have to carry it, because a vision they wrote holds up under pressure, and one handed down to them falls apart at the first bad week.

Then you tie it to measurable success criteria in the charter, so that when somebody says "on track," everyone can check against the same thing. And you keep it current. Visions go stale the way bread does, quietly, and then all at once.

How the exam asks it. For "build a shared vision" questions, pick the answer that involves the team and key stakeholders and ties the vision to success criteria. A memo from the PM or a borrowed mission statement is the distractor.

The ECO's R1 asks you to assess the project's needs, complexity, and magnitude and then recommend a development approach: predictive, adaptive or agile, or hybrid. The exam itself is built around that choice. About 40 percent of its items are predictive and about 60 percent are agile or hybrid, and they're spread through every domain.

Predictive suits work where the requirements are well understood early, change is expensive, and the physics or the regulator won't negotiate. You plan it up front, baseline it, and control changes against the baseline. A departure stage is that kind of work. You don't iterate your way to a pressure vessel. Adaptive suits work where you learn what's needed by building and showing it, change is cheap, and feedback is fast. Flight software with an astronaut as the customer is that kind of work, at least until it has to fly.

Most real projects are hybrid. The trick is the seams. In a hybrid plan the agile teams work in short iterations, and the predictive plan fixes the dates where their work has to meet the hardware: interface freezes, integrated tests, the day the code has to be on the vehicle. Those meeting points live in one integrated plan that everybody can see. If each half picks its own approach and reconciles later, "later" turns out to be the integration test, and that's the most expensive place in the project to find out you disagreed.
PMI calls fitting the method to the situation tailoring, and it expects you to do it. You tailor the process. You don't tailor away the controls that keep people alive.
How the exam asks it. Expect a scenario with stable hardware and changing software. The best answer is usually hybrid, with the integration points defined in the overall plan.
When the answer takes twenty minutes.

The ECO's P8 is plan and manage communication. Its enablers are a good checklist: define a communication strategy, promote transparency and collaboration, establish a feedback loop, understand reporting requirements, create reports aligned with what sponsors and stakeholders need, and support the reporting and governance processes.

Sam has a communication problem nobody on Earth has had to solve at this scale. A message to the station takes between three and twenty two minutes to arrive, depending on where the planets are, and for about two weeks around solar conjunction it may not arrive at all. A weekly live call with the station's engineers can't be held at all, so the strategy has to be asynchronous by design: written questions, recorded answers, a shared decision log both ends can read, agreed turnaround times, and a way to confirm that the other side understood. That last part is the feedback loop. Without it you've sent information. You haven't communicated.
None of that is special to Mars, by the way. Every distributed team has some version of the delay. Ours just has a number on it you can't argue with.
How the exam asks it. When the scenario has time zones or delays, the best answer designs communication around them. Forcing everyone into one live meeting is the distractor.
Assess before you act, and the culture you walked into.

When you inherit a project already moving, the PMI answer is the same nearly every time: assess before you act. Read what exists. Talk to the people closest to the work. Form your own picture of where things really stand. The R9 enablers say it as assess current progress, identify and tailor the artifacts you need, and communicate status. You can't communicate a status you haven't assessed, and the green slide you inherited is somebody else's assessment, made under somebody else's pressure.

B7, support organizational change, starts with an enabler that sounds soft and isn't: assess organizational culture. A project manager walked out of Sam's program on a Friday. That's a fact about Bea Kowal, and it's also a fact about the room she walked out of. Before Sam changes anything, he ought to know what that room rewards, what it punishes, and what people there have learned not to say. You can't fix a culture you haven't looked at, and you can't look at it from the head of the table.

How the exam asks it. For "what should the PM do first" on an inherited project, choose the option that gathers information before deciding. Announcing, rebuilding, or escalating on day one is the trap.
The exam tests the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, and the story will lean on it, so here are the lines that matter this week.

2.2.3 says we accept only assignments consistent with our background, experience, skills, and qualifications. Its comment covers the case Sam's in: a stretch assignment. If you take one, you make sure the key stakeholders get timely and complete information about your gaps, so they can decide whether you're the right person. Sam has never run a project. That's a gap, and Hale knows it, and the readiness board ought to hear it from him.

4.3.1 and 4.3.2 are about conflicts of interest. You proactively and fully disclose any real or potential conflict to the appropriate stakeholders. Until you've disclosed it, have an approved plan to mitigate it, and have their consent, you stay out of the decisions it could bend. The comment adds the part people miss. Even if you believe you can set your divided loyalties aside, you treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict. A father running his daughter's rescue has a conflict. The Code's answer is less dramatic than resigning and more useful: tell the right people in writing, and move the decisions it could bend somewhere else.
And 5.3.1, which you'll see again: no half-truths, no information out of context, no withholding that would make what you've said misleading. "We're on track" can be every one of those at once.
That's page one. Everybody can call a hold. Write that down.
How the exam asks it. In ethics questions, disclosure comes first. The best answer usually tells the right people the uncomfortable fact and lets governance decide.

Tuesday, January 11. Sam got in at six, before the cleaning crew had finished the second floor, and sat down at Bea's desk because it was the only desk in the building with the whole program on it. Her monitor had a sticky note on the bezel in her square capitals: ASK W ABOUT STAND. There was a mug of pens, a box of tissues with one pulled halfway out, and a printout of the integrated master schedule, all thirty one thousand lines of it, folded open to the departure stage with a coffee ring over February 2063.

By 6:40 he'd found the status deck she'd presented on Friday. Every line on it was green. He'd also found the risk register, four hundred and twelve open risks, the newest of them added in October, and an issues log that stopped in the middle of November like somebody had put the pen down halfway through a sentence.

At 7:15 Quinn came in with two coffees and set one in front of him without asking how he took it. She'd guessed right, which he noticed. Garrett wants a plan by Friday. Hale's office wants a status by Wednesday. Rafa and Hana want to know if they still have to come to Bea's Tuesday meeting, which nobody liked, so I told them probably not.
She waited. Sam realized she was waiting for him to tell her what they were doing first.
Garrett wants a plan by Friday, and Hale wants a status by Wednesday. What should Sam do first?
A. Rebuild the integrated schedule this week, then walk the leads through it by Friday.
B. Call Hale today to warn her Friday's green status is wrong and the date's at risk.
C. Bring back Bea's Tuesday meeting this week and have each lead brief their status to the room.
D. Book thirty minutes alone with each lead and ask what the green deck from Friday leaves out.

He reads until nine. Then he puts thirty minutes on the calendar with every lead and spends most of each one being quiet. Hana tells him the departure stage is two weeks behind and the deck said green because Bea's rule was nothing goes yellow without a recovery plan attached. Rafa tells him the autonomy software is fine and the interfaces to it are a disaster. Wendell tells him to come out to the stand at night sometime and listen to it. By the end of the week Sam has three pages of notes in his crew chief handwriting, and almost none of it matches Friday's deck.

That's a go. When you inherit something already moving, assess before you act. Read what exists, then go to the people closest to the work and mostly listen. That green deck is somebody else's assessment, made under somebody else's pressure. Your first deliverable is the real status.
Wednesday, January 12. Sam asked Quinn for the program charter. She came back twenty minutes later with three things and set them on Bea's desk in a row, like evidence.

The first was Tallgrass's contract with the ARA: four hundred pages, cost plus award fee, signed in 2058. The second was a statement of work for the Breather. The third was the ARA's mandate, which turned out to be a press release.

ARES RELIEF AUTHORITY FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE NOVEMBER 4, 2058. The Ares Relief Authority today directed construction of the Halcyon relief vessel to restore and expand life support at Ares Station. "Halcyon will launch in February 2063," said Director Imogen Hale. "We will bring the station what it needs. That's a promise." Tallgrass Aerospace of Watkins, Colorado, will serve as prime contractor.
None of the three said who the program's sponsor was, what success meant besides a month, or what the person running it was allowed to decide.
Garrett read the press release over his shoulder. That's your charter. Hale said it on camera, the contract's signed, and if you need a signature on something, I'll sign it. It's my company.
Garrett says the press release is the charter. What should Sam do?
A. Run on the press release and the contract for now, and write the charter after the forecast.
B. Ask the Independent Readiness Board to draft and issue the charter for the program.
C. Draft a short charter today and have Garrett sign it as sponsor, as he's offered to.
D. Draft a two page charter this week and take it to Hale to sign as the program's sponsor.

Sam drafts a real one that week. It's two pages. Purpose: restore the station's air before its margin runs out. Success: the Breather running at Ares, the crew safely there, the window used fully, the money accounted for. Constraint: the window, which nobody can move. Sam's authority gets one short paragraph. Hale reads it in her car outside the Watkins gate, changes "fully" to "honestly," changes it back, and signs it Friday. You wrote 'which nobody can move.' Yes, ma'am. That includes me. Yes, ma'am. She almost smiles.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. The sponsor issues the charter, and the PM drafting it is normal. Even midstream it's the right move. It names who's accountable, says what success means beyond a date, and gives you authority you can point to. The ARA owns the mission and the money, so Hale is the sponsor.
Decision three. A planet on the list.

Thursday, January 13. Quinn had started a stakeholder list on the program room whiteboard in green marker, because green was the only marker that still worked. By noon it had run off the right edge and onto the wall, and nobody had told her to stop.

The ARA. Tallgrass. Eleven partner governments, each with its own space office and its own budget year. Aldergrove Fluid Systems in Pueblo, which built the departure stage's valves. The Independent Readiness Board. The crew, four of them, training between Houston and Aurora. The press, which in practice meant Simon Greaves and his Countdown to Ares feed, which forty million people watched and which Bea had refused to go on. And Families of Ares, the group for colonists' relatives, which had sent Bea forty one emails since Thanksgiving. Its chair, Frances Odum, had a son on the station.
At the very bottom, in smaller letters, Quinn had written ARES STATION (212), and under that, MARS, with a question mark.
I didn't know if it counted.
Quinn put Ares Station and Mars at the bottom, not sure they counted. How should Sam handle the stakeholders?
A. Give the families, the press, and the colony to the ARA's public affairs office to manage.
B. Turn Quinn's wall into a full register and rate each party's interest and influence.
C. Register the parties that sign or fund the work now, and add the rest once it's baselined.
D. Pick up Bea's register, which is ten months old, and add new parties as they come up.

Quinn and Sam turn the wall into a register, and that takes the afternoon. Quinn wipes MARS off the board. It's not a stakeholder. It's a constraint. It doesn't read email. It goes in the charter's constraints. Ares Station goes in the register as its own line, with Hollis Bayne as its official voice and a note in Sam's handwriting: station engineering, separately. On the power and interest grid two things are uncomfortable. The families have almost no formal power and more interest than anybody alive. And the press, low on paper, sits right next to Hale. Before he leaves, Sam calls the number on Frances Odum's last email. It goes to voicemail. He leaves a real message, his name and his cell, and says he'll call back Monday, and does.

Exactly right. Identify everyone who affects the project or is affected by it, then analyze them: interest, influence, where their engagement is and where it needs to be. The colony is the reason the project exists. The window is a constraint, so it goes in the charter. Know which is which.
Friday, January 14. The HR email came at 8:02. Bea Kowal was on medical leave, effective immediately. Please do not contact her about work matters. Her equipment would be collected.

By ten Sam had heard three versions of Bea in the hallway. She'd gotten soft. She'd never been tough enough for this job. She'd been seeing somebody about it for a year. Wendell Price, the test conductor, didn't do hallway versions. He stopped in the program room doorway with his hands in his jacket pockets.

She was in this building till two in the morning most nights since August. Her car was the only one in the lot when I came in to chill the stand. That's what happened to her. He looked at the fleece on the chair. It wasn't soft. He left before Sam could answer.
Nobody had moved the fleece. Sam hadn't either.
Bea's on medical leave, and the hallway has three versions of why. What's Sam's best move?
A. Ask HR to pass Bea three questions about her files, to answer whenever she's ready.
B. Send Bea a short personal note with no work in it, then ask the leads what bad news costs here.
C. Tell the team Bea's leave is a private health matter and ask them to get back to work.
D. Respect HR's request, leave Bea alone, and put every hour into catching up the program.

Sam sends Bea a note anyway, with no work in it. It's four lines and asks her for nothing. That afternoon Sam asks Hana, Rafa, and Quinn the same question one at a time: what happened in that room last Friday, and what's it like to bring bad news here? Rafa laughs and says you don't. Hana is quiet for a while and then says Bea used to take the yellow lines home with her. Quinn says the night guards all knew her car. On Saturday morning Sam's phone buzzes at 7:48. Thank you. I'm okay. My sister's making me eat. Read my files. All of them.

That's a go. Two things at once. Bea is a person before she's a source, so you reach out as one and ask for nothing. And her leaving is data about the culture you just inherited. Assess it before you change anything: what this place rewards, what it punishes, and what people here have learned not to say.
Monday, January 17. The countdown clock hung over the high bay doors, two meters wide, red numbers, and it had been there since 2059. This morning it said 762 DAYS TO LAUNCH.

Sam got the leads together under it at seven, with coffee and a box of burritos from the place in Bennett, and asked the question Quinn had asked him in the car on the way in. Why is the date the date?

They knew the physics cold. Hana could draw the window on a napkin and did. Rafa could give the transfer time to the day. Wendell talked about the pad schedule at the Cape. In twenty minutes of talking nobody said the word station. Nobody said colony. When Wendell finally said those people and then stopped, the table went quiet in a way that told Sam how long it had been since anybody in this building had.
Sam asked the table why the date is the date. How should the program's vision get set?
A. Have the leads write the vision together in their own words, around the 212 people.
B. Draft a vision statement himself this weekend and have Hale send it out on Monday.
C. Frame the vision around Tallgrass winning every Mars contract that comes after this one.
D. Keep the countdown clock as the vision, with the station's name painted under the numbers.

It takes most of an hour and a second box of burritos. The words they end up with are mostly Rafa's, with Hana taking out every adjective. 212 people at Ares Station are running out of air. We build the ship that brings it to them, and we tell the truth about it while we do. Under it Quinn writes the success criteria, in numbers anyone can check. On Wednesday a printout goes up beside the clock: the station's manifest, all 212 names in eight point type. Sam walks past it twice before he lets himself look. ODUM, MALIK. OKAFOR, ADA N. When he turns around, half the second shift is pretending they didn't watch him do it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. A common vision gets built with the people who'll carry it, in their words, around who the work is for, and tied to measurable success criteria. The date is a constraint. The 212 people are the reason. Keep the vision visible and keep it current.
Decision six. Two kinds of work.

Wednesday, January 19. The argument had been running since long before Sam got the job. He'd heard it through the program room wall for two years without knowing it was the most important argument in the building.

Rafa Quintero ran flight software: sixty people in two week sprints, with a demo every other Friday and Commander Yusra Haddad on the screen from Houston, finding things. He wanted the whole program on sprints. The hardware schedule is a fiction we all agreed to believe. At least my backlog admits what it doesn't know.

Hana Iwasaki ran propulsion and, informally, everything that could explode. She wanted the software frozen. You can't iterate a pressure vessel. I need the valve commands defined by June and never touched again. Every time his team changes an interface, I requalify.
They both looked at Sam. Both of them were right about their own half, which was the whole problem.
Rafa wants the whole program on sprints, and Hana wants the software frozen. What approach should Sam set?
A. Let each team keep its own method and have Quinn merge the two schedules every month.
B. Put every team on two week sprints, hardware included, with one shared sprint review.
C. Run the whole program on the master schedule and freeze the software requirements now.
D. Baseline the hardware plan and keep the software in sprints tied to fixed interface dates.

Sam draws it on the whiteboard under Quinn's stakeholder list. Hardware runs on the integrated master schedule, baselined, under change control. Software runs sprints, with Yusra as the customer's voice. Where they touch, he writes a short list of fixed dates in red: the interface freeze for the valve commands, the first integrated simulation, the day the code goes onto the vehicle. That's a lot of red for an agile team. That's the first time anybody's promised me anything. Neither of them says yes. Neither says no, which in this building counts as a treaty.

Exactly right. Assess each deliverable and pick the approach that fits it. Hardware with long lead times and expensive change is predictive work. Software that learns from its customer is adaptive work. On a hybrid project the seams are where things fail, so you fix the integration points in one plan everybody can see.
Decision seven. Nine minutes each way.

Friday, January 21. In Bea's files Sam found the communication plan for the Breather work, and on page six the line that made him put his coffee down. Weekly requirements review with Ares Station engineering. Thursdays, 1500 Mountain. Live.

Quinn pulled the light time up on her tablet. Nine minutes and fifteen seconds today, one way. By next January it would be seventeen. In June of 2062, when Mars went behind the Sun, it would be twenty one minutes when there was a signal at all, and for most of three weeks there wouldn't be.

So a live call is, she said, and did the arithmetic with her lips moving. Every question takes nineteen minutes to get an answer, if they answer right away. And their day's forty minutes longer than ours, so our three o'clock walks all the way around their clock every five weeks. Half the time this meeting's at their 3 AM.
The Breather's control code had to be worked out with the station's own engineers, because they were the ones who'd be running it for the next twenty years.
Every question to the station takes nineteen minutes to answer. How should Sam set up the communication?
A. Route every technical question through Hollis Bayne's weekly official station report.
B. Keep the weekly live call and move it each week to land inside the station's work day.
C. Replace the live call with daily written question packets and one shared decision log.
D. Let Tallgrass engineers email the station's engineers directly whenever a question comes up.

Quinn and Rafa throw out the live call and build a new plan over the weekend. Every morning at six a packet goes out: numbered questions, each with the drawing or the code it's about attached and a line saying which decision is waiting on it. The station records its answers at the end of its shift. Both sides write into one decision log, and every answer gets a reply that starts with the question number and the words "understood as," so a misread shows up in a day instead of a month. In the plan, two weeks ahead of June 2062, Quinn writes CONJUNCTION: NO COMMANDS, NO NEW QUESTIONS, CLOSE EVERYTHING OPEN. The first packet goes out Monday. The first answer arrives Tuesday at 5:51 AM from a station engineer named Okonkwo, who has three questions of her own.

That's a go. A communication strategy starts from how the stakeholders can actually receive information. Here the delay is physics, so you design around it: written questions, recorded answers, one shared log, and a feedback loop that confirms what was understood. Plan for the blackout before it gets there.

Monday, January 24. Garrett held the all hands in the high bay at eleven, standing on a pallet jack in front of the habitat module, the way he'd done it since the company was eleven people in a hangar. Nine hundred people stood on the floor and along the catwalks. The countdown clock over his shoulder said 755.

He was good at this. He told the one about the first engine, and the one about the pronghorn that wandered into the high bay in 2049 and stood looking at a propellant tank for an hour like it was thinking about buying it. People laughed. Then he put both hands up. We are on track for February 18, 2063. I want every person on this floor to hear me say that.

Sam had two weeks of data. The departure stage was two weeks behind. The interfaces Rafa had warned him about were worse than Rafa had said. None of it said February 18 was impossible. None of it said the date was on track, either.
Afterward three people from the habitat team found him by the loading dock and asked him, quietly, whether it was true.
Garrett just told nine hundred people that February 18 holds. What should Sam do?
A. Take his two weeks of data to Garrett alone today and agree what on track means.
B. Send Hale a short note that the CEO's date is ahead of the program's data.
C. Tell the three what he knows and doesn't, and let Garrett's message stand for now.
D. Ask Garrett during the floor questions what data the February 18 date rests on.

Sam tells the three people the truth he has: nobody knows yet, and there'll be a real forecast by the end of the month. Then he takes Garrett one page. What's known, what isn't, the two weeks on the stage, the seam in the software. Garrett reads it with the smile on. I've got investors, Sam. If I stand up there and say 'we don't know,' I'm on the news. If you say 'on track' and it isn't, you're on the news in a year. So am I. They go around for forty minutes. Where they land: Tallgrass will call the window the target, and the program will publish its forecast and its confidence every month. Garrett hates the word confidence. He agrees to it anyway, and he doesn't smile when he does, which Sam decides to count as sincere.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Aligning expectations means bringing the hidden difference into the open and getting to one agreed definition. Do it privately with the senior stakeholder, bring the data, and agree on words you can both say in public. Then tell the team the same thing.

Thursday, January 27. Hale's office asked for the program's first forecast by five. She had a call Monday with all eleven partner governments. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, put the rest in writing. The Director wanted "a number she can say."

Quinn had spent two weeks with the leads, activity by activity, getting three estimates for every long piece of work, optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic, from the people who'd do it instead of from the slides. Run with those ranges, the integrated schedule said February 18, 2063 was possible and wasn't likely. The departure stage had no float at all. The software interfaces had negative float until somebody fixed the seam. Put together, the chance of launching by the 18th came out about one in five. The chance of launching somewhere inside the window, before it closed in early March, came out a little better than half.

And there was the other number, the one on the back of the gas bill. Every date in the plan assumed the ARA's oxygen model. If the model was sixty days optimistic, the schedule could be perfect and still arrive too late.
He had Hale's signed charter in the folder. It said success was air at Ares, and it called the window a constraint.
Sam owes Hale the program's first forecast. What should he do?
A. Give February 18 as the committed date and report the risks against it each month.
B. Send Hale the date ranges, their odds, and the oxygen model assumption they all rest on.
C. Forecast the close of the window in March as the date, with the ranges in an appendix.
D. Ask Hale for sixty more days to firm up the estimates before any forecast goes out.

The page is short. Launch by February 18: about one in five. Launch inside the window: a little better than half, as of today. The three things driving it, in order. The two moves that would raise the odds the most: fixing the software seam this quarter and buying back float on the departure stage. And one line under risks, in plain words. The program's schedule assumes the ARA's oxygen margin model; station engineering data he has seen runs lower; he recommends the agency verify the model independently before the partners' call. Hale calls him at 6:40. I can't say 'a little better than half' to eleven governments. You can say the window's the target and we'll give them the odds every month. They'll believe the month after that one. A long pause. Who's seen this station data? I have. Fine. I'll ask for the check. On Monday she tells the partners the window is the target and the program's confidence is moderate and will be reported monthly. Nobody hangs up.

Exactly right. A forecast is collected data plus honest analysis: ranges, how likely they are, what drives them, and what would change them. Name the critical information the plan rests on, here the oxygen model, and ask for it to be verified. Give the sponsor options and let her decide what to say.
Saturday, January 29. Ruth Calder lived in Golden, in a narrow house above Clear Creek, with a two car garage that held, according to the board's clerk, a telescope and no cars.

Sam had asked for twenty minutes with any member of the Independent Readiness Board. Ruth was the one who said yes, on the condition that he come to her, because she didn't drive out to Watkins anymore and didn't say why.

She was seventy four, small, with short white hair and a cardigan with a pen clipped in the pocket. The pen was green. Her kitchen table had a newspaper on it, an actual paper one, and a green cloth binder with the cover shut and her hand resting flat on top of it, as if it might get up.
I'm not your mentor, she said, before he'd sat down. I sit on the board that decides whether your ship flies. That's a different job, and I only do one at a time. What do you want?

He'd come to ask how the board wanted to be told things. Sitting across from her, he understood the question was bigger. There was a fact about him the board needed to hear, and he'd been letting everyone assume it was handled because everyone already knew it.
Sam is sitting in a board member's kitchen. What's his best move?
A. Ask Ruth to give him an early look at the board's questions before each review.
B. Offer to step aside as program lead and ask Ruth whom the board would want instead.
C. Write down that his daughter is on the station and give the page to Ruth and Hale.
D. Ask Ruth how the board wants status reported, in what format, and how often.

He writes it on her notepad, in front of her, because she seems like the kind of person you do that in front of. A conflict of interest, disclosed: his daughter, Ada Okafor, lives on Ares Station. Then the mitigation. Any decision that accepts risk to crew safety, any closure of a criticality 1 anomaly, and any change that touches the colony's margin goes to the board with his recommendation and the data, and the board decides. He doesn't. He'll send the same page to Hale on Monday. Ruth reads it twice. Most people in your chair think 'everybody knows' counts as telling. She uncaps the green pen and adds a line under his: He can call a hold any time. He can't call one off. Then she opens the binder, takes out the first page, and slides it across the table. I'm still not your mentor. No, ma'am. Read it in the car.

That's a go. Code 4.3.1 says disclose real or potential conflicts proactively and fully to the right people, and 4.3.2 says stay out of the decisions it could bend until there's a mitigation plan and consent. "Everybody knows" isn't disclosure. Write it down, and set escalation thresholds so the decisions it touches go above you.

Tuesday, February 1. The ARA's briefing room in Denver had blue curtains and the agency seal on the wall and smelled of carpet glue. Hale wanted Sam at the podium beside her for the program's first public update since Bea.

Her communications director had written his line on an index card. Halcyon remains on schedule for launch on February 18, 2063. Under it, in pencil, someone had added: mention your daughter? personal touch.

Simon Greaves sat in the second row with a camera drone folded on his knee like a sleeping bird. Behind him, by the wall, a woman in a red coat held a framed photograph of a teenage boy against her chest. Sam knew who she was before anybody told him. He'd been leaving her voicemails for two weeks.
Hale leaned over. Read the card. Smile when you say Ada.
Sam has been handed a card to read. How should he handle it?
A. Ask Hale to let him say the team's vision and call the window the target instead.
B. Read the card with one added line of his own warning that the date is aggressive.
C. Read the card as written and tell Ada's story, the personal touch the note asks for.
D. Let the communications director read the update and keep the program out of the cycle.

He has ninety seconds before they walk out. He shows her the team's two sentences and says he'll call the window the target and promise to report the odds every month. And your daughter? She's one of the 212. That's the only way I'll say it. Hale looks at him the way she'd look at a vote count. Fine. At the podium he reads the two sentences. Greaves asks whether Halcyon will meet February 18. Sam says the window is real, the date inside it is a forecast, and he'll tell them every month how it's looking. Greaves writes something down. At the back of the room the woman in the red coat lowers the photograph a few inches.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Promoting a shared vision means saying in public what the team says inside, and keeping it current as the facts move. The vision is the 212 people and the window. Using his daughter as a talking point would make one colonist matter more than the rest, and every family would notice.

Thursday, February 3, eight at night. Sam sat at the kitchen table with the tablet propped against the fruit bowl. The gas bill was still under it, face down. One way light time tonight was eight minutes and eight seconds. Ada would get whatever he said in her morning, at breakfast, and she'd watch it twice, because she always did, and she'd hear every single thing in it he didn't mean to put there.
He'd been recording logs at this table for two years. He knew which chair had the best light. It was Grace's. He'd never sat in it to record, and he didn't now.

Over the counter, on the pantry door frame, were the pencil marks from when Ada was two until she was fifteen and refused to stand there anymore. Every one had a date beside it in Grace's handwriting, until the last three, which were in his.

He pressed record. The red light came on. Everything he knew was in his head at once: about one in five for the 18th, Bea in a parking lot in Bennett, the oxygen model he'd asked the agency to check, the job, and the job's reason, which was her.
Ada watches every log twice and hears what he doesn't mean to say. What should Sam tell her?
A. Keep it light and tell her they're on track, and save the hard parts for later.
B. Wait to record until the monthly forecast is out and send her the real number then.
C. Give her the real odds for the 18th and a promise to send them every month.
D. Attach everything he has: the forecast, the ARA briefing, and his notes on Bea.

He tells her he has the job. He tells her the date is a forecast and not a promise, gives her the odds, about one in five for the 18th, and says he'll send them every month whether they're good or bad. He tells her he read her 952 three times and he's taking it seriously, and he leaves out what isn't his to tell. He doesn't do the voice. Near the end he says, Your mom's coffee maker is dying, and I'm not replacing it. Don't argue with me. You're ninety one million miles away and I'll win. He sends it. Eight minutes and eight seconds later it's on Mars, waiting for her.

Exactly right. Building trust with a stakeholder means telling them the truth in a form they can use and promising a cadence you'll keep. Protect what isn't yours to share, like Bea's privacy and the agency's internal papers. Give Ada what she asked for: a real number and a father who doesn't do the voice.

At 10:40 he called Tucson. Ray Mendez, his old flight chief, answered on the second ring, the way he had for twenty years, as if he'd been sitting beside the phone, which Sam had long suspected he was.
Saw you on that Greaves thing, Ray said. You didn't read the card. I could tell. You've got a face for when you're not reading the card.

Sam told him about the gas bill. He hadn't told anyone else. He read Ray both numbers and the difference, and Ray was quiet long enough that Sam took the phone away from his ear to see if the call had dropped.
I told her the odds. Good. She'd have heard it if you didn't. She heard it when she was thirteen.
For what it's worth, you sound like a man who did it right this week. You never sound happy when you do.

Listen. The jet doesn't care how you feel. You know that. Doesn't mean you don't get to feel it. Means you do the forms right anyway, and then you go feel it in the truck. A pause, and the sound of a screen door in Tucson. Go to bed, Okafor.

Ruth's page was on the refrigerator under the magnet shaped like Colorado, where he'd put it after reading it twice in her driveway with the engine running. SHORT VERSION: EVERYBODY. WRITE THAT DOWN, RUTHIE. He knew about the Petrel the way everybody on a flight line that summer did: the squadron break room TV, three people, June 2035, something in the departure burn. He hadn't known until Saturday that the flight director had a first name a person could call her by.

Read my files, Bea had written. All of them. He'd been through the program folders twice. At 11:52 he found the one he'd missed, because it wasn't in the program folders at all. It was on her personal share, sorted to the bottom of the list, the only folder in there named in capitals.
Inside was one scanned report and a photo of a manila folder with handwriting across the tab.

Anomaly report AR 2207, on the Halcyon departure stage's main oxidizer isolation valve, MOIV-1, Aldergrove part 7740-112. In acceptance test on Monday, August 18, 2059, cycle 3 of 5, its position readings disagreed at the close command for 40 milliseconds, and two attempts to repeat it were normal. It was downgraded from criticality 1 to 2 as suspected test stand noise, on a recommendation in review minutes that aren't in the file, so flight rule 2.36 didn't apply. Closed UNR, unexplained, not repeatable, on Friday, September 19, 2059. Approved, B. Kowal, program manager.

He knew what the date meant before he checked it, and he checked it anyway. Eleven days before the September 30 schedule review. He'd sat in the back of that review. He remembered it as the one where everything was green.
Then the photo. Bea's square capitals, the same hand as the sticky note on her monitor, in blue ballpoint across the folder tab. I SIGNED IT. I SHOULDN'T HAVE. SOMEBODY HAS TO OPEN IT AGAIN.

The rule number meant nothing to him, so he looked it up. ARA Flight Rules, section 2, rule 36: no criticality 1 anomaly may be closed as unexplained without three independent attempts to reproduce it and the flight director's signature. Originator: R. Calder, March 2036. Carried into the ARA book in 2056.

He looked over at the refrigerator for a while. Then back at the line that said two attempts, and the line above it where somebody had turned a 1 into a 2, and the name at the bottom. Read together they made a sound he'd heard before, the way an engine you've known for years sounds the first morning something's wrong with it.

Under the fruit bowl the gas bill said minus seventeen. On the screen the report said closed. It was 12:06, Friday now, and the wind had come up off the plains and was working at the back door the way it did, and the neighbor's motion light clicked on for nothing at all.
